newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin tells Russian military to explain reforms.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin tells Russian military to explain reforms.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, hitting back at critics of his controversial military reforms, told Russia's defence minister on Monday to launch a publicity campaign to explain the shake-up.

Yeltsin summoned Defence Minister Igor Sergeyev to the Volzhsky Utyos resort in central Russia where he is on holiday to discuss reforms announced last week, including cutting troop numbers by 500,000 to 1.2 million by the end of 1998.
Some senior military figures, led by sacked defence minister Igor Rodionov and former Kremlin security aide Alexander Lebed, have savaged the reform plans.

"People need to know the true content of the reforms, and politicians need to know, so that they can make the right judgements about the first reform measures and steps," Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin as saying.
"Do you really have no authoritative specialists in the defence ministry who could have explained to people how the reform began and how it is going?" he asked.
Sergeyev replied: "They were biding their time".
Yeltsin, who is commander-in-chief of the armed forces, suggested military experts should be enlisted in propaganda work and even go on television to preach the message of reform.
Defying his critics, he said he was sticking to plans to create a fully professional, non-conscript army.

His military reform plans have been criticised at every turn and Lev Rokhlin, head of the lower house of parliament's defence committee, has set up a non-military organisation to defend the armed forces' interests.
The president gave short shrift to Rokhlin. "We will brush aside the Rokhlinites with their unconstructive actions. We do not need such help," he said.

Despite his comments, independent military experts say Rokhlin's new movement has worried the Kremlin and was partly responsible for Yeltsin pushing ahead with reforms and vowing to settle wage arrears to the military by the start of September.

Rokhlin said last week the army was being destroyed "catastrophically quickly". Rodionov said Yeltsin's approach to reforms was a destabilising factor and Lebed said he was not optimistic the reforms would succeed.

The 66-year-old president wants to turn the armed forces into a smaller and more efficient fighting force after years of declining standards which culminated in humiliation at the hands of separatists in Chechnya in a 21-month conflict.

Many servicemen have not been paid for months, some have nowhere to live and morale has sunk. Military spending has fallen in real terms and the defence ministry says it does not even get all the funds set aside for it in the budget each year.
After many stalled attempts at reform, Yeltsin signed decrees last week outlining the first major steps, including merging some units and making cutbacks across the board.
Giving more details of the reforms on Monday, Yeltsin said the number of army generals would gradually be reduced to a maximum of 2,300, indicating the cutbacks would also affect the top brass.

He said great attention would be paid to the needs of servicemen who are discharged. He said the state would pay for 50,000 flats to help them and regional leaders would be asked to provide another 50,000.
